title: Ang 537: Bihagra begins
tomorrow: what does longing sound like when it can't sleep?

cards: At night the questions get bigger. Where am I going? Does any of this make sense?
Is anybody steering? Bihagra, a raga tradition sings at night, opens on ang 537 with Guru Tegh Bahadur saying it flatly: nobody knows the Lord's ways.
Yogis, ascetics, and plenty of clever people have worn themselves out trying. So if nobody can know, why keep trying? Sikhs answer that in more than one way.

teach.b: First the hymn, in paraphrase: no one knows the Lord's ways.

Yogis, celibates and ascetics have exhausted themselves, and so have many clever people. In an instant he turns a beggar into a king, and a king into a beggar. He fills what's empty, and empties what's full.
That's the night raga's opening: not an answer, but a longing that knows it won't be answered on its own terms. Now, the two ways people read it.
One reading says: stop grasping. The best case is right in the text. The cleverest people wore themselves out.
Knowing was never the way in. What's left is to let go, take refuge, and trust the One whose ways you can't map.
The other reading says: keep seeking. Its best case is the Granth itself. The Gurus knew no one could know, and they kept singing anyway, page after page, raga after raga.
Not-knowing doesn't make the search pointless; it makes it endless. You can want what you can't hold. Both readings agree on one thing: the longing stays.
Neither one says quit. Only how to carry it: with open hands, or with open eyes.

how: Sikhs reading the Granth in order reach Bihagra after Devgandhari; tradition sets the raga at night, and its hymns and chhants are sung in kirtan.

s: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Bihagra hymn says no one knows the Lord's ways
yogis, ascetics and many clever people have worn themselves out trying.
the hymn's point is that seeking God is pointless
readers differ on how to carry it, letting go or seeking on, but neither says quit.
in the hymn, the Lord can turn a king into a beggar in an instant
and a beggar into a king; he fills the empty and empties the full.

games.q: your friend says: if no one can know God's ways, why study the Granth at all? you think study matters. what's the strongest case for her side?
o: the hymn says the clever wore themselves out; knowing was never the way in.
studying is only for scholars, so ordinary people can skip it.
the Granth doesn't really teach anything about God.
games.why: her best case is the text: yogis, ascetics and clever people wore out. yours is the Granth itself: the Gurus kept singing anyway.

practice: Close your eyes, or lower them, and let one big question come up, the kind that shows up at night. Don't answer it. Sit with the wanting-to-know itself for the whole sit; if you'd like, read the ninth Guru's hymn on ang 537 first.

wordCard.voice: Ang 537. Where Bihagra begins, with the ninth Guru saying no one knows the Lord's ways, not even the clever.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gat, state or way; 'har kee gat', the Lord's ways, which no one knows (ang 537).

carryVoice: Night longing: wanting what you can't fully know, and staying with it anyway. Sleep well when it's time.
